## Problem 1 - NHANES Audiometry

### (a) Import and merge data

```{r}
library(foreign)

aux <- read.xport("data/AUX_I.xpt")
demo <- read.xport("data/DEMO_I.xpt")

nhanes <- merge(aux, demo, by = "SEQN", all = FALSE)

dim(nhanes)
```

The two datasets are merged by the respondent identifier SEQN.
Only respondents appearing in both datasets are retained.
The merged dataset contains 4,582 observations and 119 variables.

### (b) Clean variables

```{r}
nhanes$gender <- factor(
  nhanes$RIAGENDR,
  levels = c(1, 2),
  labels = c("Male", "Female")
)

nhanes$citizenship <- factor(
  nhanes$DMDCITZN,
  levels = c(1, 2),
  labels = c("US citizen", "Not US citizen")
)

table(nhanes$gender, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes$citizenship, useNA = "ifany")
```

Gender and citizenship are converted to labeled factors.
Refused and unknown citizenship responses are treated as missing.

```{r}
nhanes$children <- nhanes$DMDHHSZA

nhanes$children[!nhanes$children %in% 0:3] <- NA

table(nhanes$children, useNA = "ifany")
```

The number of children aged five or younger is kept numeric,
with 3 representing three or more children.

```{r}
income_codes <- c(1:10, 14, 15)

income_labels <- c(
  "$0-4,999",
  "$5,000-9,999",
  "$10,000-14,999",
  "$15,000-19,999",
  "$20,000-24,999",
  "$25,000-34,999",
  "$35,000-44,999",
  "$45,000-54,999",
  "$55,000-64,999",
  "$65,000-74,999",
  "$75,000-99,999",
  "$100,000+"
)

nhanes$income_category <- factor(
  nhanes$INDHHIN2,
  levels = c(income_codes, 12, 13),
  labels = c(
    income_labels,
    "$20,000+ (broad category)",
    "Under $20,000 (broad category)"
  )
)

nhanes$income_score <- match(
  nhanes$INDHHIN2,
  income_codes
)

table(nhanes$income_category, useNA = "ifany")
table(nhanes$income_score, useNA = "ifany")
```

Income codes 14 and 15 represent the highest brackets, so the
twelve nonoverlapping brackets are scored from 1 to 12 in
increasing income order. Codes 12 and 13 describe overlapping
ranges; they are retained as labeled categories but excluded
from the numeric score. Refused and unknown responses are
treated as missing.

### (c) Poisson regression models

```{r}
for (v in c("AUXTWIDR", "AUXTWIDL")) {
  nhanes[[v]][nhanes[[v]] %in% c(555, 777, 888)] <- NA
}

model_1R <- glm(
  AUXTWIDR ~ gender,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

model_2R <- glm(
  AUXTWIDR ~ gender + citizenship + children + income_score,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

model_1L <- glm(
  AUXTWIDL ~ gender,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

model_2L <- glm(
  AUXTWIDL ~ gender + citizenship + children + income_score,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

models <- list(
  "1R" = model_1R,
  "2R" = model_2R,
  "1L" = model_1L,
  "2L" = model_2L
)
```

```{r}
# Extract IRRs from a fitted Poisson model.
# Inputs: model and model name. Output: coefficient IRR table.
get_irr <- function(model, model_name) {
  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Term = names(coef(model)),
    IRR = exp(unname(coef(model)))
  )
}

irr_results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(models), function(name) {
    get_irr(models[[name]], name)
  })
)

knitr::kable(
  irr_results,
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Exponentiated coefficients for the four Poisson models"
)
```

Exponentiated slope coefficients represent ratios of expected
tympanometric widths, holding other covariates fixed.
The exponentiated intercept is the baseline expected width.

```{r}
# Summarize sample size and model fit.
# Input: fitted Poisson model and model name.
# Output: one-row data frame of N, McFadden pseudo-R2, and AIC.
get_model_stats <- function(model, model_name) {
  y <- model.response(model.frame(model))

  null_model <- glm(
    y ~ 1,
    family = poisson(link = "log")
  )

  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    N = nobs(model),
    McFadden_R2 = 1 -
      as.numeric(logLik(model)) / as.numeric(logLik(null_model)),
    AIC = AIC(model)
  )
}

model_stats <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(models), function(name) {
    get_model_stats(models[[name]], name)
  })
)

knitr::kable(
  model_stats,
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Sample sizes and model fit statistics"
)
```

McFadden's pseudo-R-squared is calculated as $1 - \ell_{\text{model}}/\ell_{\text{null}}$. Each null model uses the same observations as its corresponding fitted model.

### (d) Gender comparison in model 2L

```{r}
gender_result <- summary(model_2L)$coefficients["genderFemale", ]

gender_result
exp(coef(model_2L)["genderFemale"])
```

I tested whether the female-to-male IRR equals 1. The estimated
IRR is 1.0187 (z = 5.160, p = 2.47e-7), so I reject the null
hypothesis at the 5% level under the Poisson model. Holding
citizenship, number of young children, and income score fixed,
the expected left-ear tympanometric width is about 1.87% higher
for females than for males.

```{r}
comparison <- data.frame(
  gender = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = levels(nhanes$gender)),
  citizenship = factor(
    rep("US citizen", 2),
    levels = levels(nhanes$citizenship)
  ),
  children = 0,
  income_score = 6
)

comparison$predicted_width <- predict(
  model_2L,
  newdata = comparison,
  type = "response"
)

knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

For US citizens with no children aged five or younger and an
income score of 6 ($25,000–34,999), the predicted widths are
85.397 for males and 86.998 for females, a difference of about
1.601. Because the model has no gender interactions, equal
predicted means correspond to an IRR of 1. The same Wald test
therefore provides evidence of a difference in predicted means
under the Poisson model (p = 2.47e-7).

## Problem 2 - Sakila

```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(microbenchmark)

con <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(),
  "data/sakila_master.db"
)

dbListTables(con)
```
### (a) Customers by store

```{r}
# Extract customer records and summarize them in R.
# Input: open database connection.
# Output: customer count and active percentage for each store.
customers_R <- function(con) {
  customers <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT store_id, active FROM customer"
  )

  groups <- split(customers, customers$store_id)

  do.call(rbind, lapply(groups, function(x) {
    data.frame(
      store_id = x$store_id[1],
      customers = nrow(x),
      active_percent = 100 * mean(x$active == 1)
    )
  }))
}

answer_a_R <- customers_R(con)

knitr::kable(
  answer_a_R,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Customer summary using SQL extraction and R"
)
```
```{r}
sql_a <- "
  SELECT store_id,
         COUNT(*) AS customers,
         100.0 * AVG(active) AS active_percent
  FROM customer
  GROUP BY store_id
  ORDER BY store_id
"

answer_a_SQL <- dbGetQuery(con, sql_a)

knitr::kable(
  answer_a_SQL,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Customer summary using a single SQL query"
)

benchmark_a <- microbenchmark(
  R = customers_R(con),
  SQL = dbGetQuery(con, sql_a),
  times = 30L
)

knitr::kable(
  summary(benchmark_a, unit = "ms"),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Execution times in milliseconds"
)
```

Both methods give the same results. Store 1 has 326 customers,
of whom 97.55% are active, while Store 2 has 273 customers,
of whom 97.44% are active. In this benchmark, the single SQL
query has a lower median execution time than extracting the
data and calculating the results in R.

### (b) Staff names and countries

```{r}
# Extract and join staff location tables in R.
# Input: open database connection.
# Output: staff names and countries, ordered by staff ID.
staff_R <- function(con) {
  staff <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT staff_id, first_name, last_name, address_id FROM staff"
  )
  address <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT address_id, city_id FROM address"
  )
  city <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT city_id, country_id FROM city"
  )
  country <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT country_id, country FROM country"
  )

  result <- merge(staff, address, by = "address_id")
  result <- merge(result, city, by = "city_id")
  result <- merge(result, country, by = "country_id")

  result <- result[order(result$staff_id), ]
  result[c("staff_id", "first_name", "last_name", "country")]
}

answer_b_R <- staff_R(con)

knitr::kable(answer_b_R, row.names = FALSE)
```
```{r}
sql_b <- "
  SELECT s.staff_id, s.first_name, s.last_name, co.country
  FROM staff AS s
  JOIN address AS a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
  JOIN city AS ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
  JOIN country AS co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
  ORDER BY s.staff_id
"

answer_b_SQL <- dbGetQuery(con, sql_b)

knitr::kable(answer_b_SQL, row.names = FALSE)

benchmark_b <- microbenchmark(
  R = staff_R(con),
  SQL = dbGetQuery(con, sql_b),
  times = 30L
)

knitr::kable(
  summary(benchmark_b, unit = "ms"),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Execution times in milliseconds"
)
```

Both methods identify Mike Hillyer in Canada and Jon Stephens
in Australia. The single SQL query has a lower median execution
time than extracting the four tables and joining them in R.

### (c) Films with the highest total rental revenue

```{r}
# Calculate total payments per film using R.
# Input: open database connection.
# Output: film(s) tied for the highest total rental revenue.
revenue_R <- function(con) {
  payment <- dbGetQuery(
    con, "SELECT rental_id, amount FROM payment"
  )
  rental <- dbGetQuery(
    con, "SELECT rental_id, inventory_id FROM rental"
  )
  inventory <- dbGetQuery(
    con, "SELECT inventory_id, film_id FROM inventory"
  )
  film <- dbGetQuery(
    con, "SELECT film_id, title FROM film"
  )

  result <- merge(payment, rental, by = "rental_id")
  result <- merge(result, inventory, by = "inventory_id")
  result <- merge(result, film, by = "film_id")

  result$cents <- round(100 * result$amount)
  totals <- aggregate(cents ~ film_id + title, result, sum)

  highest <- totals[totals$cents == max(totals$cents), ]
  highest$total_revenue <- highest$cents / 100

  highest <- highest[order(highest$film_id), ]
  highest[c("film_id", "title", "total_revenue")]
}

answer_c_R <- revenue_R(con)

knitr::kable(
  answer_c_R,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Films with the highest total rental revenue (USD)"
)
```
```{r}
sql_c <- "
  WITH revenue AS (
    SELECT f.film_id, f.title,
           SUM(CAST(ROUND(100 * p.amount) AS INTEGER)) AS cents
    FROM payment AS p
    JOIN rental AS r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
    JOIN inventory AS i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film AS f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    GROUP BY f.film_id, f.title
  )
  SELECT film_id, title, cents / 100.0 AS total_revenue
  FROM revenue
  WHERE cents = (SELECT MAX(cents) FROM revenue)
  ORDER BY film_id
"

answer_c_SQL <- dbGetQuery(con, sql_c)

knitr::kable(
  answer_c_SQL,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE
)

benchmark_c <- microbenchmark(
  R = revenue_R(con),
  SQL = dbGetQuery(con, sql_c),
  times = 30L
)

knitr::kable(
  summary(benchmark_c, unit = "ms"),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Execution times in milliseconds"
)
```

Both methods identify TELEGRAPH VOYAGE (film ID 879) as the
film with the highest total rental revenue, at $231.73.
I calculated revenue by summing the recorded payments linked
to each film's rentals. In this benchmark, the single SQL query
has a lower median execution time than the R approach.
All timings include data extraction and calculation but exclude
opening the database connection. Performance may vary between runs.


## Problem 3 - Australian Records

### (a) Websites ending in .com

```{r}
au <- read.csv(
  "data/au-500.csv",
  colClasses = "character"
)

dim(au)

web_host <- sub(
  "[/:?#].*$", "",
  sub("^https?://", "", tolower(trimws(au$web)))
)

is_com <- grepl("\\.com$", web_host)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    com_websites = sum(is_com),
    total = nrow(au),
    percentage = 100 * mean(is_com)
  ),
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE
)
```
None of the 500 websites ends in .com, so the percentage is 0%.
All websites end in .com.au, which is excluded by the matching rule.

### (b) Most common email domain

```{r}
email_domain <- tolower(sub("^.*@", "", au$email))

domain_counts <- sort(
  table(email_domain),
  decreasing = TRUE
)

top_domains <- domain_counts[
  domain_counts == max(domain_counts)
]

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    domain = names(top_domains),
    count = as.integer(top_domains)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The most common email domain is hotmail.com, appearing in
114 of the 500 records.

### (c) Nonalphabetic characters in company names

```{r}
nonalpha <- grepl(
  "[^[:alpha:],[:space:]]",
  au$company_name
)

nonalpha_no_amp <- grepl(
  "[^[:alpha:],[:space:]&]",
  au$company_name
)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    rule = c(
      "Exclude commas and whitespace",
      "Also exclude ampersands"
    ),
    count = c(sum(nonalpha), sum(nonalpha_no_amp)),
    proportion = c(mean(nonalpha), mean(nonalpha_no_amp))
  ),
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Excluding commas and whitespace, 45 company names (9%) contain
a nonalphabetic character. Also excluding ampersands reduces
this to 4 company names (0.8%).

### (d) Phone number formatting

```{r}
# Format phone numbers using cell-phone-style grouping.
# Input: character vector of ten-digit phone numbers.
# Output: character vector formatted as 1234-567-890.
cell_format <- function(phone) {
  digits <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", phone)

  stopifnot(all(nchar(digits) == 10))

  paste(
    substr(digits, 1, 4),
    substr(digits, 5, 7),
    substr(digits, 8, 10),
    sep = "-"
  )
}

au$phone1 <- cell_format(au$phone1)
au$phone2 <- cell_format(au$phone2)

knitr::kable(
  head(au[c("phone1", "phone2")], 10),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Both phone columns are reformatted as 1234-567-890.
The first ten records show the new format, with leading zeros
preserved.

### (e) Histogram of log apartment numbers

```{r}
has_apartment <- grepl("[0-9]+\\s*$", au$address)

apartment <- as.numeric(sub(
  ".*?([0-9]+)\\s*$",
  "\\1",
  au$address[has_apartment],
  perl = TRUE
))

positive_apartment <- apartment[apartment > 0]

length(positive_apartment)

hist(
  log(positive_apartment),
  breaks = "FD",
  col = "lightblue",
  border = "white",
  main = "Log apartment numbers",
  xlab = "Natural logarithm of apartment number"
)
```

I extracted 130 positive apartment numbers from the ends of
addresses and plotted their natural logarithms. The histogram
has its highest frequency between 4 and 6, with fewer observations
toward either end. Addresses without a trailing number and
nonpositive values are excluded.

### (f) Benford's law

```{r}
leading_digit <- as.integer(
  substr(as.character(positive_apartment), 1, 1)
)

observed <- table(factor(leading_digit, levels = 1:9))
benford_prob <- log10(1 + 1 / (1:9))

benford_table <- data.frame(
  digit = 1:9,
  observed_proportion = as.numeric(observed) / sum(observed),
  expected_proportion = benford_prob
)

knitr::kable(
  benford_table,
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE
)

barplot(
  rbind(benford_table$observed_proportion, benford_prob),
  beside = TRUE,
  names.arg = 1:9,
  col = c("steelblue", "orange"),
  legend.text = c("Observed", "Benford"),
  args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n"),
  xlab = "Leading digit",
  ylab = "Proportion"
)

benford_test <- chisq.test(observed, p = benford_prob)
benford_test
```

The apartment numbers do not appear to follow Benford’s law. The digit 1 occurs in only 9.23% of the numbers, compared with the expected 30.10%, while digit 9 occurs in 14.62%, compared with 4.58%. A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test gives $\chi^2(8) = 62.268$, $p = 1.67 \times 10^{-10}$, so I reject the null hypothesis that the leading digits follow Benford's distribution. These numbers would therefore fail a Benford-based screening. However, apartment numbers are assigned identifiers and may not follow Benford’s law even in real data, so this result alone does not prove that they are artificial. In this case, the data source explicitly identifies the records as synthetic.
